messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar Haddad was 30 when he was referred for treatment, a divorced Middle Eastern American man who worked as a tax inspector and had begun to organize his life around not being inside a moving vehicle. The collision had happened at night after he left a work-related dinner where several people had been drinking. Omar had not been drinking himself, but he remembered the sharp smell of alcohol inside the other car and on the breath of the man who staggered on the roadside afterward. What stayed with him most was the instant before impact: headlights veering where they should not have been, the shape of a car like the one that struck him filling his windshield, and the conviction that there was no time left to do anything useful. In recounting it, he returned to the image rather than a full narrative, as if the event existed in flashes: the car coming at him, metal folding, a loud cracking sound, and that heavy alcohol smell mixed with airbag dust.

In the weeks after the crash, Omar found that certain moments seemed to pull that scene directly into the present. Passing a damaged car on the road could stop him cold; he said it was not simply that he remembered the crash, but that the image arrived all at once, vivid and close, as if he were back in front of the windshield waiting for impact. If he caught the smell of alcohol on someone in a grocery line or outside a restaurant, his body tightened before he had time to think. Similar cars were especially difficult. When he noticed one in traffic or parked near his apartment complex, he would stare at it, already braced, scanning its dents, its angle, the person getting in. He had become convinced that ordinary attention was no longer enough, that he had to stay on guard because danger could appear in an instant and because, in his view, he had already learned what happened when he failed to anticipate it.

That sense of threat spread into daily life. Unexpected or loud sounds made him jump hard enough to embarrass him at work. A dropped file in the office, a door slamming in the hallway, a car horn outside the county building where he conducted inspections could send a jolt through him. He described himself as superalert all day, always listening for something sharp or sudden. Colleagues noticed that he startled easily and laughed it off as stress, but Omar experienced it as proof that something in him had changed. He had come to believe he could no longer rely on himself. Before the collision he had thought of himself as competent, careful, and steady, someone who managed details for a living and took pride in being dependable. Now he was certain those qualities no longer protected him, and he questioned whether he was capable of doing the things that had defined him as an adult man living independently after his divorce.

Because driving or even riding in a car felt intolerable, Omar began arranging his days around avoidance. He delayed field visits, traded assignments when he could, and made excuses about scheduling conflicts rather than explain that being a passenger was nearly as bad as driving himself. When in-office duties were available, he clung to them. On days when travel was unavoidable, he became tense hours beforehand and sometimes cancelled at the last minute. This started to affect how he was seen at work; a job that had once rested on mobility and routine site visits became harder to perform, and Omar privately took that as more evidence that he was no longer capable.

Outside work, he spent long stretches on his phone, gaming or scrolling late into the night because silence left too much room for the crash imagery to return. He described it less as enjoyment than as escape, a way to keep his mind occupied until he was exhausted enough to sleep. He also began eating less. Sometimes he skipped meals entirely, saying that restricting food gave him a strange sense of control on days when he otherwise felt detached and ineffective. His routines narrowed. Friends invited him out, but he often declined if it meant riding with someone else, and even when he did go, the smell of alcohol in bars or on people passing by made him want to leave immediately.

What distressed him most was not only fear, but a deadened quality he felt in himself. He said he no longer trusted his own reactions and was afraid he would never feel normal emotions again. Even moments that should have brought relief or pleasure seemed flattened. By the time he sought help, the strain had become difficult to hide: work travel was a recurring problem, his eating had become irregular enough that he felt run down, and whole evenings disappeared into his phone while his life seemed to shrink around him. He came in after realizing that a routine sight on the road—a wrecked car being towed, a smell of beer from a man walking past, the glimpse of a car like the one from the crash—could still overtake him so completely. What he wanted, cautiously, was to feel like himself again. What frightened him was the possibility that the man he had been before the collision was gone for good.
